btos.label: Real estate and rental and leasing (NAICS 53)

name: Real Estate
blurb: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest AI and now federally regulated under FHFA and CFPB quality-control rules; plus valuation, leasing, and property-management platforms with methodology disclosed.

points.desc: Census BTOS reports real-estate sector AI use directly from firms.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.name: AVMs are now federally regulated AI

points.desc: The bureau's AVM rule page and its algorithmic-appraisal work are the record of how valuation bias and model accountability are supervised.

points.name: Opendoor prices houses with models at risk

points.name: CREtech and MetaProp track the proptech market

points.name: BOMA covers commercial building operations

summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
AI adoption in real estate has reached 31.9% of firms as of the Census Bureau's latest survey, up from 28.9% in the prior period, reflecting accelerating integration across residential and commercial segments. The sector's AI deployments concentrate in three distinct layers: valuation and pricing at the consumer and institutional level, operational automation in property and lease management, and data infrastructure connecting buildings to digital intelligence.

Valuation models are the sector's oldest and most regulated AI systems. Zillow publishes Zestimates for over 110 million homes using neural network architectures trained on county records, MLS data, and historical sales, while institutional investors rely on platforms like HouseCanary, which provides valuations and forecasts for 136 million U.S. properties through machine learning analysis of real estate data from thousands of sources. These models now operate under federal oversight: the FHFA, CFPB, OCC, Board, FDIC, and NCUA jointly adopted quality control standards for automated valuation models used in mortgage origination and securitization, mandating policies, procedures, and control systems to ensure confidence in AVM estimates, prevent data manipulation, and avoid conflicts of interest through random sample testing and reviews. This regulatory framework reflects the stakes embedded in valuation AI, where pricing errors accumulate into balance-sheet losses for firms like Opendoor, which uses proprietary models to set cash offers on residential homes.

Commercial real estate and property operations are automating through document intelligence and conversational AI. Prophia extracts lease terms, rent rolls, and risk signals from commercial lease documents using AI combined with expert validation, helping owners and operators structure portfolio data for management and decision-making. EliseAI deploys agentic conversational AI to handle tenant messages, maintenance requests, tour scheduling, and lead follow-up automatically across housing and healthcare operations, while Building Engines' Prism platform runs property management workflows end-to-end, using AI to deliver instant answers and recommendations that cut costs and improve net operating income. JLL, the largest commercial real estate services firm, reports investing more in AI technology than any other real estate company, unlocking value across brokerage, portfolio management, and facilities work.

Residential brokerage and consumer-facing tools integrate AI into agent workflows and buyer-seller matching. Compass applies machine learning to listing recommendations and client matching, while Matterport's 3D capture and computer vision digitize buildings into immersive tours and floor plans, reducing site visits and enabling remote portfolio management. The National Association of Realtors operates the REACH program, a technology scale-up platform run by Second Century Ventures, the most active venture fund in global real estate technology, signaling where the profession's capital and attention concentrate.

Proptech capital and professional adoption remain concentrated among CREtech members, institutional investors tracked by CRETI and MetaProp, and the major brokerages and services firms. NAR, BOMA, and industry conferences bring together operators actively deploying AI, though most deployment announcements emphasize cost reduction and efficiency rather than quantified ROI. The regulatory landscape for valuation AI is now binding through federal AVM standards, while day-to-day automation in leasing, operations, and communication faces no equivalent federal rule, leaving each vendor and operator to implement controls independently. For firms evaluating AI deployment, the sector's evidence points toward strong adoption momentum in valuation and operations, established vendor offerings with transparent methodologies in some cases, and regulatory expectations around model quality in mortgage-related AI that will likely extend to other high-stakes decisions over time.

https://www.consumerfinance.gov/rules-po.brief: The CFPB, OCC, FRB, FDIC, NCUA, and FHFA adopted a final rule establishing quality control standards for automated valuation models used by mortgage originators and secondary market issuers when assessing collateral value on mortgages secured by a consumer's primary residence. Under the rule, institutions must implement policies and control systems to ensure AVMs produce reliable estimates, guard "against the manipulation of data," and avoid conflicts of interest. The standards require random sample testing and reviews of the models used in credit decisions and securitization determinations.
